analysis.title: THINK Ahead: Your questions, answered
key_insights: ING's base case is more dovish and benign than market pricing. It expects oil prices to fall further, easing inflation and letting central banks stop hiking after a final rate hike in December.

Weaker household balance sheets limit pass-through from higher energy prices to core inflation. Companies absorb the cost by squeezing profit margins. Major central banks could consider rate cuts towards the end of 2027.

Beyond 12 months, market rate expectations are virtually flat. The current curve resembles the 2007 hiking cycle, not 2008 or early 2023, when markets priced a much larger decline in rates after the near-term peak.

ING sees two conditions that would produce a more humped curve with a lower terminal rate: a material growth slowdown (the 2008 ECB policy error is the extreme case) or lower inflation risks. Growth remains robust, so ING does not see the first as likely in 2027.
ING considers the inflation-decline path more likely and expects markets to reprice to a lower ECB rate by mid-2027, as happened after inflation peaked in 2023.

Higher energy prices hit lower-income eurozone households harder, but Europe's social safety net protects them. The consumer-confidence gap between the top and bottom income quartiles has not widened in 2026.
The eurozone savings rate has fallen since energy prices began rising, cushioning consumption. Rising unemployment expectations make further declines in the savings rate unlikely.

US fiscal position: interest costs are 4% of GDP and the primary deficit is 2.5% of GDP. Midterm results lock in the primary deficit, with President Trump likely to veto Democratic tax and spending policies.

With an average borrowing cost of 3.6%, nominal GDP must grow 6.1% a year to hold debt-to-GDP at 100%. Nominal growth is closer to 5%, so the ratio looks set to climb. An AI-driven productivity boom that lifts growth and lowers interest costs would change this.

The ECB will be hesitant to restart bond purchases while governments do not adopt austerity, because QE risks weakening fiscal discipline. If the French fiscal crisis spreads while the rest of the eurozone keeps to fiscal rules, the ECB is likely to start the Transmission Protection Instrument to ring-fence France.

The quits rate is the best leading indicator for US wages. It peaked at 3% in 2022 with wage growth at 5.5%. It is now 2% with wage growth at 3%, a low-hire, low-fire economy, so national wage growth stays benign until quits rise.

ING expects a cautious Fed on cuts for much of 2027, so monetary policy is not a strong early-year tailwind for gold. Rising easing expectations, lower yields and a softer dollar, plus central bank buying and geopolitical uncertainty, should support gold in 2027, with volatility in periods of higher yields and dollar strength.
US week ahead (Knightley): a shortened Thanksgiving week follows hefty falls in stocks and bonds driven by anxiety over the AI outlook and potential Fed hikes.

US core PCE deflator (Wednesday) is expected to come in hot given the CPI and PPI already published. ING forecasts 0.3% MoM against the 0.17% MoM needed to track 2% YoY over time. GDP is unlikely to be revised much from the initial 3.4% print.
Consumer confidence may get a lift from large falls in gasoline and diesel prices, but weak wage growth, job security concerns and lower household wealth limit the upside.

tension_points.bull_case: ING's base case is that oil falls further, core inflation pass-through is limited because companies absorb costs in margins, and central banks stop hiking after December and consider cuts towards end-2027. Markets would reprice to a lower ECB rate by mid-2027.
tension_points.bear_case: Markets price virtually no cuts beyond 12 months, with a curve like the 2007 hiking cycle. A hot core PCE print and potential Fed hikes are weighing on stocks and bonds.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A material slowdown in the growth outlook would also lower the terminal rate, while robust growth with persistent inflation risks would keep the curve flat.

tension_points.bull_case: An AI-driven productivity revolution could boost growth and tax revenue, lower inflation and let interest costs fall, which would change the debt-to-GDP outlook dramatically.
tension_points.bear_case: Nominal GDP growth near 5% is below the 6.1% needed to hold debt-to-GDP at 100%, with a locked-in 2.5% primary deficit and interest costs at 4% of GDP.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Nominal GDP growth reaching 6.1% a year or more would stabilise debt-to-GDP at 100%.
